title: August and the Letter
premise: In 1899, in the port city of Valdorra on the eve of revolution, Felix Sandoval — a young woman living as her late father's son to keep the family print shop — hides dissident pamphlets in the type cases of the letterpress trade. When a census taker notices the discrepancy between the shop's records and its resident, Felix and her found family of printers must flee with nothing but what they can carry: one tray of movable type. Their flight becomes a race to print and distribute the true account of a massacre the government is already rewriting, culminating on New Year's Eve 1900 when Felix sets the final page by hand as soldiers breach the pressroom — and the truth escapes into the crowd before the century turns.
about_author: Jonah Underhill is the pen name of a former compositor who spent fifteen years setting type for regional newspapers before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about people whose names were never meant to survive the record.

chapters.title: The Weight of Sorts
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. We meet the Sandoval print shop through Felix's hands: measuring type, measuring flour, measuring what can be carried. Her father is dead; she lives as his son to keep the license. The emotional beat is quiet competence masking fear of discovery.

chapters.title: One Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Census taker Aurelio Voss arrives, meticulous and oddly sympathetic, and asks why the shop's apprentice has no birth record under his name. Felix lies badly. That night she finds Voss's card slipped under the door with a printed line from a banned pamphlet — he knows, and has not reported her.

chapters.title: The Massacre at Salt Quay
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Felix and dockworker Marisol Reyes, who witnessed soldiers fire on striking stevedores. The official gazette calls it a riot begun by the workers. Marisol comes to the shop at midnight asking for the truth to be set in type. Emotional beat: terror hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: Composing Stick
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV centered on the print shop family — old proofreader Teo, Marisol, Felix. They typeset the eyewitness account overnight while patrols pass the windows. Felix realizes the census form Voss filed could either bury or protect them. Beat: found family forged in shared risk.

chapters.title: What the Census Knows
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. He is ordered to correct his 'error' regarding the Sandoval household. Torn between career and conscience, he alters the record to list Felix as her father's daughter — an act that makes him complicit. He warns them: the archive will be seized within days. Beat: betrayal of institution, loyalty to persons.

chapters.title: Carry Only What Prints
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Soldiers come early. The family flees with one type case, the locked massacre account, and Marisol's testimony. Teo stays behind to burn the incriminating proofs and is arrested. Beat: grief and guilt carried alongside the lead.

chapters.title: The Underground Press
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. In the cellars beneath the tannery district, Felix meets the scattered network of printers who have been waiting for something worth printing. Distrust runs high — everyone suspects informers. Felix must prove herself by recutting a damaged letterform from memory. Beat: earning belonging.

chapters.title: Victors' Historians
chapters.summary: Voss's POV, now inside the government archive where official history is being rewritten to erase Salt Quay entirely. He steals the original casualty ledger and brings it to the underground press, knowing it ends his life as it was. Beat: the state's power over memory made explicit.

chapters.title: Setting the Final Page
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, climax. New Year's Eve 1900. With soldiers sweeping the district toward the tannery, the press runs the full account — massacre, ledger, names of the dead. The press jams on the last signature; Felix sets the final lines by hand as boots sound on the stairs. Beat: desperate, sacred craft under threat.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, resolution. The pamphlets flood the midnight crowds; copies travel on ships before dawn. Teo returns from prison months later; Voss vanishes into exile but sends one letter — set in their own type. Years on, historians cite 'the Sandoval printing' as the surviving record. Beat: quiet triumph; identity no longer hidden but chosen.
